## In brief

Substitution is the power tool of single-variable integration; its two-dimensional version is **change of variables**. The catch: when you swap $(x,y)$ for new coordinates $(u,v)$, the area element does not carry over unchanged — a small tile $dx\,dy$ is stretched into a differently-sized tile $du\,dv$, and the stretch factor is the **Jacobian**. For a *linear* change, that factor is just the determinant of the coefficient matrix (rescaling $x/a,\,y/b$ turns the unit disk into an ellipse and multiplies areas by $ab$, giving $\text{area}=\pi ab$). For a general, curving change, the same is true *locally*: linearize the map, and the local area stretch is $\big|\det J\big|$ where $J=\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)$, so that $du\,dv=\big|\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)\big|\,dx\,dy$. The two Jacobians of a map and its inverse are **reciprocals**, and — the satisfying part — feeding in $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta$ reproduces exactly the $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$ we took on faith last lecture.

## 1. The concepts

### 1.1 Warm-up: the area of an ellipse

The ellipse with semi-axes $a,b$ is $\big(\tfrac{x}{a}\big)^2+\big(\tfrac{y}{b}\big)^2\le 1$. Rescale into $u=\tfrac{x}{a},\ v=\tfrac{y}{b}$; the ellipse becomes the **unit disk** $u^2+v^2\le 1$. Since $x=au,\ y=bv$, a step $dx=a\,du$ and $dy=b\,dv$, so $dx\,dy=ab\,du\,dv$. Therefore
$$
\text{area}=\iint_{\text{ellipse}} dx\,dy
= ab\iint_{\text{unit disk}} du\,dv
= ab\cdot \pi = \pi a b .
$$
The whole trick is that flattening the region to something trivial costs a **constant area factor** $ab$, which we pull out front.

### 1.2 The general question

Sometimes we change variables to simplify the **region** (ellipse $\to$ disk), sometimes to simplify the **integrand** (e.g. $u=3x-2y,\ v=x+y$). Either way the one thing we must pin down is the relationship between the old area element $dA=dx\,dy$ and the new one $dA'=du\,dv$. Everything else is bookkeeping.

### 1.3 Linear changes: the determinant is the area factor

Take a **linear** map, say $u=3x-2y,\ v=x+y$. A small rectangle in the $(x,y)$-plane maps to a **parallelogram** in the $(u,v)$-plane. From the two edge vectors of the image parallelogram, its area is the absolute determinant of the coefficient matrix:
$$
\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}3 & -2\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\right| = |3+2| = 5 .
$$
So $du\,dv = 5\,dx\,dy$, and because the map is linear this factor is the **same everywhere** — it doesn't depend on which rectangle you picked. Reading it the other way for integration,
$$
\iint \cdots\,dx\,dy=\iint\cdots\frac{1}{5}\,du\,dv .
$$

### 1.4 The Jacobian: linearize, then take the determinant

For a **general** (curving) change $u=u(x,y),\ v=v(x,y)$, the factor is no longer constant — but *locally* every smooth map looks linear. Small displacements transform by the matrix of partial derivatives:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}\Delta u\\ \Delta v\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}u_x & u_y\\ v_x & v_y\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\ \Delta y\end{pmatrix}.
$$
A small rectangle in $(x,y)$ becomes a small parallelogram in $(u,v)$ whose area is $\big|\det[\,\cdot\,]\big|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y$. That determinant is the **Jacobian**:
$$
\boxed{\;J=\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\det\begin{pmatrix}u_x & u_y\\ v_x & v_y\end{pmatrix},
\qquad du\,dv=\left|\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\right|dx\,dy\;}
$$
The absolute value is there because area is positive regardless of orientation.

### 1.5 The two Jacobians are reciprocals — and polar is the sanity check

A map and its inverse have reciprocal Jacobians:
$$
\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}\cdot\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=1,
$$
so you compute whichever one is easier. **Polar coordinates** are the reassuring test. With $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta$,
$$
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}
=\det\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & \ \ r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}
= r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta = r .
$$
So $dx\,dy=|r|\,dr\,d\theta=r\,dr\,d\theta$ — precisely the area element we *asserted* in Lecture 17, now **derived**.

### 1.6 A worked example: $u=x,\ v=xy$

Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 x^2y\,dx\,dy$ by changing to $u=x,\ v=xy$. Three steps.

**① Area element.** $\displaystyle\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\det\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ y & x\end{pmatrix}=x$, so $du\,dv=x\,dx\,dy$ (with $x\ge 0$), i.e. $dx\,dy=\tfrac1x\,du\,dv$.

**② Integrand.** $x^2y\,dx\,dy=x^2y\cdot\tfrac1x\,du\,dv=xy\,du\,dv=v\,du\,dv$ (since $v=xy$).

**③ Region.** The unit square maps to a triangle: $u=x\in[0,1]$, and $v=xy$ runs from $0$ up to $x=u$, so $0\le v\le u\le 1$. Hence
$$
\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 x^2y\,dx\,dy
=\int_0^1\!\!\int_{v}^{1} v\,du\,dv
=\int_0^1 v(1-v)\,dv=\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\frac16 ,
$$
matching the trivial direct computation $\big(\int_0^1 x^2dx\big)\big(\int_0^1 y\,dy\big)=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac16$.

## 2. The key intuition

**A change of variables re-draws the grid, and the Jacobian is the exchange rate on area.** When you move to $(u,v)$, the neat unit squares of the $(x,y)$-grid get bent and stretched into curvy quadrilaterals; integration only cares about how much **area** each little cell holds, so before you can add up $f$ over the new grid you must convert cell-areas from old currency to new. That exchange rate is $\big|\det J\big|$: it is the factor by which the map inflates or shrinks a tiny patch right there. It is *local* because a curving map stretches unevenly — a lot in some places, little in others — and the determinant of the linearization captures the stretch *at that point*. For a straight-line (linear) map the stretch is uniform, so the Jacobian is a single constant (the $5$, the $ab$). The beauty is the self-consistency: apply the machine to $x=r\cos\theta,\,y=r\sin\theta$ and out drops the $r$ we had merely believed before — the "extra $r$" of polar was a Jacobian all along.

## 3. Python demonstration

### 3.1 The Jacobian really is the local area-stretch factor

Rather than trust the determinant formula, we **measure** the stretch geometrically. Map the four corners of a tiny cell through $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta$, compute the image quadrilateral's area with the shoelace formula, and divide by the original cell area. The ratio should be $r=\big|\det \partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)\big|$ — a check that never invokes the Jacobian formula it is verifying.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

to_xy = lambda r, t: (r*np.cos(t), r*np.sin(t))          # polar map (r,θ) -> (x,y)
def shoelace(xs, ys):                                    # polygon area from its vertices
    return 0.5*abs(np.dot(xs, np.roll(ys, -1)) - np.dot(ys, np.roll(xs, -1)))

eps = 1e-4
for r0, t0 in [(0.5, 0.3), (1.0, 1.0), (2.0, -0.7)]:
    corners = [(r0, t0), (r0+eps, t0), (r0+eps, t0+eps), (r0, t0+eps)]
    xs = np.array([to_xy(r, t)[0] for r, t in corners])
    ys = np.array([to_xy(r, t)[1] for r, t in corners])
    measured = shoelace(xs, ys) / eps**2                 # geometric area stretch
    print(f"(r,θ)=({r0:>3},{t0:>4}): measured stretch {measured:.5f}   |det J| = r = {r0:.5f}")
    assert abs(measured - r0) < 1e-2
print("Jacobian = local area-stretch factor ✓  (this is exactly dx dy = r dr dθ)")
```

### 3.2 Change of variables leaves the integral unchanged

Two integrals, each computed the transformed way and checked against an independent direct method.

```{python}
# (a) ellipse area = π a b  via  u = x/a, v = y/b
a, b = 3.0, 2.0
cov_ellipse = a*b*np.pi                                  # ab * area(unit disk)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
M = 4_000_000
X = rng.uniform(-a, a, M); Y = rng.uniform(-b, b, M)
mc_ellipse = ((X/a)**2 + (Y/b)**2 <= 1).mean() * (2*a)*(2*b)   # independent MC, no substitution
print(f"ellipse : change-of-var πab = {cov_ellipse:.5f}   Monte Carlo = {mc_ellipse:.5f}")
assert abs(cov_ellipse - mc_ellipse) < 0.05

# (b) ∬_square x²y dx dy  via  u=x, v=xy  →  ∬ v du dv over 0≤v≤u≤1
K = 1500
grid = (np.arange(K) + 0.5) / K
U, V = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
cov_val = V[V <= U].sum() * (1.0/K)**2                   # transformed integral ∬ v du dv
Xg, Yg = np.meshgrid(grid, grid)
direct = (Xg**2 * Yg).sum() * (1.0/K)**2                # independent: direct ∬ x²y dx dy
print(f"x²y     : change-of-var ∬ v du dv = {cov_val:.5f}   direct ∬ x²y dx dy = {direct:.5f}  (= 1/6)")
assert abs(cov_val - 1/6) < 1e-3 and abs(direct - 1/6) < 1e-3
print("change of variables leaves the integral unchanged ✓")
```

The picture shows *why* the transformed integral is easy: the curvy grid of the $(x,y)$ square straightens into a plain triangle in $(u,v)$.

```{python}
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 4.4))

# left: unit square in (x,y) with the level lines u=x (vertical) and v=xy (hyperbolas)
for uc in np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10):
    axL.plot([uc, uc], [0, 1], color="#1f6fb2", lw=.9)
for vc in np.linspace(0.1, 0.9, 9):
    xs = np.linspace(vc, 1, 120)
    axL.plot(xs, vc/xs, color="#c8641e", lw=.9)
axL.plot([0, 1, 1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1, 1, 0], "k-", lw=1)
axL.set_title(r"$(x,y)$: lines $u=x$, hyperbolas $v=xy$", fontsize=10)
axL.set_xlim(0, 1.05); axL.set_ylim(0, 1.05); axL.set_aspect("equal")
axL.set_xlabel("x"); axL.set_ylabel("y")

# right: image region in (u,v) — the square has become the triangle 0 ≤ v ≤ u ≤ 1
for uc in np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10):
    axR.plot([uc, uc], [0, uc], color="#1f6fb2", lw=.9)
for vc in np.linspace(0.1, 0.9, 9):
    axR.plot([vc, 1], [vc, vc], color="#c8641e", lw=.9)
axR.plot([0, 1, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1, 0], "k-", lw=1)
axR.set_title(r"$(u,v)$: the square becomes $0\leq v\leq u\leq 1$", fontsize=10)
axR.set_xlim(0, 1.05); axR.set_ylim(0, 1.05); axR.set_aspect("equal")
axR.set_xlabel("u"); axR.set_ylabel("v")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 4. Feynman test

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Prompt**: your friend knows $u$-substitution for single integrals but is surprised that in 2-D you can't just replace $dx\,dy$ by $du\,dv$. Explain what the Jacobian is, why it's needed, and why it's a *determinant*. Then close the loop: what is the "extra $r$" in polar coordinates, really?

**My answer**: *A change of variables is really just re-drawing the plane with a new coordinate grid. There's no reason a patch of area should stay the same size in the new grid — the map twists, stretches, or squeezes it. So we need a stretch factor: how much a tiny piece of area in the old grid becomes in the new one. That factor is the Jacobian.*

*Here's the thing that dissolves the surprise: this factor was already there in 1D. When your friend does a $u$-substitution, they don't really swap $dx$ for $du$ — they write $dx = \frac{dx}{du}\,du$, dragging along the derivative $\frac{dx}{du}$. That derivative is a Jacobian; they just never called it that. In 1D you're stretching a length, so one number (a derivative) does the job. In 2D you're stretching an area, so you need the 2D version of the same idea.*

*Why a determinant, specifically, and not just the product of two stretch factors? Because the two new grid directions needn't be perpendicular — the map can shear them, tilting one toward the other. Tilt the sides of a square without changing their lengths and its area shrinks, yet a plain product of side-lengths wouldn't notice. The tool that measures the true area of a parallelogram spanned by two vectors — shear and all — is the determinant (exactly what we saw back in Lecture 2, where it collapses to zero when the two vectors line up flat). Since the stretch factor is really "the area of the little parallelogram the map produces," it has to be a determinant.*

*And the punchline: the mysterious "extra $r$" in $dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta$ is nothing but this Jacobian for the polar map. Far from the origin, the same $d\theta$ sweeps a wider arc, so the cells grow with $r$ — and the determinant of the polar map records exactly that. The "weird" polar area element was a Jacobian all along.*
:::

## 5. Pitfalls & takeaways

- **You cannot just swap $dx\,dy$ for $du\,dv$.** The area element transforms; the missing factor is $\big|\det J\big|$. This is the single idea of the lecture.
- **Absolute value, always.** $du\,dv=\big|\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)\big|\,dx\,dy$. Orientation can flip the sign of the determinant, but area is positive.
- **Pick the Jacobian that's easy, then invert if needed.** $\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)$ and $\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)$ are reciprocals; compute whichever one has the simpler partials and take $1/{\cdot}$ if you need the other.
- **Transform the region too.** New variables mean new limits — re-read the boundary in $(u,v)$ (here the unit square became the triangle $0\le v\le u\le 1$). A right integrand over the wrong region is still wrong.
- **Linear maps have a constant factor; curving maps don't.** For $u=3x-2y,\ v=x+y$ the stretch is $5$ everywhere; for polar it is $r$, which varies. Don't assume a single number unless the map is linear.
- **Polar is a special case, not a separate rule.** $r\,dr\,d\theta$ *is* a Jacobian. Once you see that, every "weird area element" becomes the same one recipe.
